newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bonn's EMU confidence intact, deficits a worry.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bonn's EMU confidence intact, deficits a worry.

text.p: Bonn's government left no doubt on Thursday that Germany fully intended to qualify fairly and squarely for monetary union, but a Portuguese newspaper said even the European Commission now doubts this is possible.

Amid growing uncertainty as to whether Germany can rein in its budget deficits to hit a target of three percent of gross domestic product this year, two Bundesbank officials warned that the single currency should not be bought at any cost.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and French president Jacques Chirac, at a meeting late on Wednesday, reaffirmed their commitment to creating a single currency on time in 1999 and pledged to stick by the strict entry criteria for entry.

The leaders' political intentions were underscored on Thursday by Finance Minister Theo Waigel and his deputy Juergen Stark, who stressed in speeches in Ludwigsburg and Berlin that Germany would rein in its budget deficit to achieve EMU entry.

"Germany will fulfil the criteria," Waigel told a savings bank conference. "Even current developments give no cause to veer from these forecasts. But should there still be a need to act, we will not hesitate to do what is necessary."
Stark, speaking at a breakfast meeting in Berlin hosted by a local group of Kohl's Christian Democrat party, insisted the economic criteria for EMU must be strictly adhered to.
"The criteria were not anchored in the Maastricht Treaty only for us then to depart from them. We want to take them seriously and we must take them seriously," he said.
"We shall meet the deficit criterion. There is no doubt about that...I don't know where this doubt is coming from."

Countries which wish to meld their currencies into the euro from 1999 must meet targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation, public debt and budget deficits this year in advance of a 1998 decision on which nations will take part.

Germany, in common with many other European nations, is facing most problems in reaching the deficit goal of three percent of gross domestic product. Its forecast for a deficit of 2.9 percent this year is deemed optimistic by many analysts.

Fresh doubts about Bonn's ability to qualify on the deficit target without resorting to excuses -- such as the heavy cost burden of German unification -- emerged after a newspaper unveiled a higher forecast from the European Commission.

Portugal's Publico said new forecasts showed that Germany's deficit would total 3.2 percent of GDP in 1997 -- the crunch year for EMU qualification. A representative from the newspaper said the figures had been obtained from the Commission, which is due to release revised forecasts on April 23.
A Commission spokesman declined to comment on their accuracy. "Work on the forecast is still continuing," he said.

Doubts about the Germany's ability to meet the criteria also emanated from the Bundesbank council, as Reimut Jochimsen, who heads the regional central bank based in Dusseldorf, said it would be tough for Germany to fulfil the fiscal criteria.
"It is becoming increasingly evident, that Germany will find it extraordinarily difficult to meet the budget and debt criteria," Jochimsen told Germany's monthly magazine Die Neue Gesellschaft.
Jochimsen also said that any delay in the planned January 1, 1999 start date laid down in the Maastricht Treaty could not be categorically ruled out.
The question of delay should not be made taboo, or made into a question of "war and peace" the magazine reported Jochimsen as saying in an interview.

Separately, a second Bundesbank council member, Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher, said the problems that nations were having in meeting the criteria presented the risk that those criteria would end up being interpreted "too generously".

"I am quite clearly opposed to any such attempt to start European currency union at any price," he said, adding that only a "clear and strict" interpretation of the criteria would lend the project credibility.
But he cautioned:"...To me it is extremely questionable whether a postponement would lead to any improved (economic) convergence (between nations)," he said.
Moreover, the credibility of a new, politically-determined start-date would "indeed be slight", he added.
